source.title: Egalitarian Gradient Descent: A Simple Approach to Accelerated Grokking

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some entries in the flattened Table 4 are malformed or incomplete.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks and tests whether changing the gradient update accelerates it. This is a conceptual test, not a replication of the original grokking method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training/test learning curves and epochs or steps to specified accuracy thresholds for algorithmic tasks and MNIST. The CIFAR-10 label-shuffling experiment measures recovery after distribution shifts, not grokking, so it is not included as a row. Results cited from other papers are not included.
record.test_reason: The study reports train/test learning curves under baseline and modified optimizers, directly testing delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks and MNIST. Its toy analysis also tests initialization-dependent plateaus. These are behavioral results, beyond a comparison of optimizer performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors attribute delays to unequal progress along gradient principal directions and propose spectral normalization to shorten or remove plateaus. The exact analysis concerns simplified linear settings; neural-network evidence is empirical. They report acceleration on algorithmic tasks and MNIST, exact-SVD instability on the transformer, and rank-dependent performance for randomized SVD.
record.recipe_differences: This is an optimizer-intervention study, not a reproduction of the original training recipe. It compares vanilla SGD with EGD, randomized-SVD EGD, and column normalization, with additional comparisons to Grokfast.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome and speed vary with optimizer/update method and randomized-SVD rank. Exact-SVD EGD is described as unstable on the modular-multiplication transformer; randomized SVD is reported stable there. In the toy setting, vanilla-GD plateau length varies with initialization scale, while EGD is reported insensitive to that scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: EGD improves recovery of training accuracy after CIFAR-10 label shuffling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient spectral normalization can improve adaptation to changing labels; training-accuracy recovery does not measure delayed held-out generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: EGD and vanilla SGD reach different parameter-space regions on modular arithmetic, with more convergent trajectories on sparse parity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice changes parameter trajectories and endpoints; this does not identify whether the learned algorithms differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Modular-addition hidden-layer gradients have ill-conditioned spectra at the beginning and end of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient spectral conditioning is associated with optimization delays; these endpoint spectra do not measure gradual formation or removal of identifiable circuits.

record.problems: The main learning curves are figures rather than numerical tables. The parity Table 4 is malformed in the provided flattened text, and some entries cannot be safely assigned. Several comparisons report threshold epochs without uncertainty estimates. The smaller-training-set delay trend in V1 is not tested.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted additional randomized-SVD rank results from Appendix C, Tables 2-4, retaining the listed baselines, exact-SVD EGD, selected rank variants, and the explicit parity column-normalization failure. Omitted wall-clock-time and per-epoch-time metrics in those tables because they do not measure the grokking behavior. Omitted the MNIST final-validation-accuracy column from Table 6 and the CIFAR-10 label-shuffling area-under-curve results because they are not direct measures of delayed generalization.

untested.parts: A controlled training-set-size sweep showing that the post-memorization delay grows as the training set shrinks. Changing the modulus at fixed data ratio also changes task size and class count.
Identifiable generalizing circuits forming gradually, later removal of memorizing components, and circuit progress measures anticipating the jump.

Initialization or weight-norm interventions on MNIST itself; weight-norm control; a lazy-to-rich transition; text and molecules. The toy initialization result is not evidence of nonlinear feature learning.
Delayed generalization during realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning. The transformer experiment is small-scale modular arithmetic.
Circuit efficiency under low-norm bias, critical dataset size, and ungrokking. Using weight decay does not test this account.
Identification and comparison of learned algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters. Different parameter trajectories do not establish different algorithms.

Adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits as causes of the baseline delay, and removal of the delay by controlling those artifacts. Spectral preconditioning is a different intervention.

missing.what: Equal-distribution toy result: Theorem 2 gives a plateau of order 1/(eta epsilon) when both stated conditions hold, and no plateau if either fails; Figure 8 compares vanilla GD and the modified update. This is an additional conditional result, not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for the supplied versions. Threshold times must be interpreted alongside train/test curves, since they do not alone establish grokking or measure its delay. The parity values selected in the record are readable despite malformed neighboring entries. No circuit-level or numerical-artifact verdict follows from optimizer acceleration.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not sweep training-set size to test whether smaller training sets require more optimization.
It does not measure gradual formation of an identifiable generalizing circuit, later removal of memorizing components, or circuit-based progress measures anticipating the jump.
It reports MNIST results and a synthetic toy initialization-scale analysis, but does not test weight-norm control, a lazy-to-rich transition, text, or molecules.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
Weight decay is used in experiments, but the paper does not test the efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below it.
The paper does not identify algorithms learned across runs or test whether runs converge to the same algorithm.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits as the cause of grokking delays, or whether controlling those factors removes the delay.
